title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit
description: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers a
body: The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move."During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident."So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice. "I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit."I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X."Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

schema.headline: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit

title: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
description: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetime
body: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe. Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer."Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. "However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples."It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements. "That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade."With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities. He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres. He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space. "We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here."I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

schema.headline: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss

title: Prince George to start school at Eton College
description: Prince George set for first day at Eton CollegeImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince George, pictured last month, will follow in his father's fo
body: Prince George set for first day at Eton CollegeImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince George, pictured last month, will follow in his father's footsteps at EtonByRoyal correspondentPrince George is taking another step in growing up with his first day at Eton College.He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, who also attended the historic school in Berkshire.The 13-year-old prince will become a boarder at the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around £65,000 a year.As the oldest child of Prince William and Catherine, George is second in line of succession to the throne.Image source, Kensington Palace/Matt PorteousImage caption, A photograph of Prince George was released for his 13th birthdayThere had been speculation about which school Prince George would attend when he finished at independent prep school Lambrook in Berkshire, with a number of private schools being suggested.But a traditional option was chosen, with Prince George following his father, uncle Prince Harry, and great uncle Earl Spencer in attending Eton College.Prince George will now become a boarder, with the school having 25 boarding houses, with each having approximately 55 pupils, looked after by residential staff headed by a house master.The school is also not far from the prince's family home in Windsor.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince William on his first day at Eton in 1995"Some boys take to boarding like a fish to water; others take a minute to settle in," writes the Good Schools Guide about Eton College, which says the school provides each boy with a private single room.Melanie Sanderson, the school guide's managing editor, said Eton has "spectacular facilities and spacious grounds"."Yet despite its ancient buildings, it is a modern school with a progressive outlook."Most 13-year-old boys arriving there in September cannot possibly know what adult life holds for them."Prince George, however, faces a very particular future and his parents, with an unrivalled choice of schools available to them, have decided that an Eton education represents the best preparation for life as a modern working royal," she said.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, William's mother, father and brother, plus house master, on his first day at EtonImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince Harry, with his father and housemaster, arrived at Eton on a rainy day in 1998Among recent politicians to have attended Eton have been Lord David Cameron, Boris Johnson, Kwasi Kwarteng and Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.Old Etonian celebrities include Eddie Redmayne, Dominic West, Damian Lewis and Tom Hiddleston.Prince William, interviewed when he was aged 18, had spoken of enjoying his time at Eton."I've really enjoyed being able to go about Eton as just another student," he said in June 2000.

schema.headline: Prince George to start school at Eton College

title: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says
description: Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to
body: Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC). In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.  HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report also highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing. Skeer said it was a "pivotal moment for policing" and said "there are still areas where performance is not good enough"."If managed correctly, I firmly believe that reform presents a significant opportunity to deliver a better service for both the public and those working within policing," she added.The HMIC report said that evolving crime and threats mean officers deal with more complex and resource-intensive cases.But the government's planned reforms, including the creation of a National Police Service to take over counter-terror and fraud investigations could alleviate some of the pressure facing local units, Skeer wrote.Policing minister Sarah Jones said: "Our plans will tackle the long-term challenges in the policing system and bring it into the modern day. "We are investing in more neighbourhood policing, raising standards and making better use of technology to make sure local policing works for local people."Responding to the report, the charity Victim Support said: "Police forces are undoubtedly under immense pressure, but they must get the basics right." Chief executive Katie Kempen added: "It is unacceptable that victims and survivors are paying the price for police failings. Every victim of crime deserves to be treated with respect, to be given access to justice, and to have their needs identified and met."Growing financial pressure is repeatedly pointed to as increasing the strain on police forces.Cleveland's police's Chief Constable, Victoria Fuller, recently told the BBC her force has been understaffed and under resourced for years."The facts are the facts," she said. "We have got the highest crime rate in the country. We've had the largest decrease in officers in the country since 2010."As a police force, if you were to look at the multiple indices of deprivation, our police force is number one. So we absolutely need more, we need more resources."An extra £2m targeted funding has since been designated to help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026-2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash.The annual HMIC report comes just months after a different publication by the Police Leadership commission found the system for identifying and developing leaders was too weak, with chief constable roles in England and Wales often attracting a single suitable candidate.The landmark independent review warned police leadership is not consistently of a high enough standard and requires a fundamental overhaul.It also pointed to low morale and motivation within the service, recommending reformed recruitment and promotion processes.Additional reporting by Dan Sales

schema.headline: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says

title: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King
description: The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.L
body: The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals."It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case."The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".Prince Harry and Meghan faced an acrimonious departure from the UK in 2020, which they chronicled in their Netflix documentary.They established their financial independence in California, including Prince Harry writing a best-selling memoir Spare and Meghan creating an online food range, As Ever.This summer the couple made a surprise return to the UK, where their children will be going to school.It's expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.Disputes about Prince Harry and Meghan's security in the UK remain unresolved and the letter spells out: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."Prince Harry has complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK, but the Palace says that has to be addressed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - which decides security for royals and public figures.Palace sources have suggested it was better to make the Lord Chamberlain's letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.Prince Harry and Meghan's representatives have been contacted for a response.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King

title: 'I performed on stage to get my first job' - the firms turning recruitment into competitions
description: Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman is on track to get a full-time job with L'OréalByMaryLou CostaYumi Liberman was up on stage in f
body: Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman is on track to get a full-time job with L'OréalByMaryLou CostaYumi Liberman was up on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience of 300 people, and she had to perform.But rather than singing, dancing or playing a musical instrument, she and two friends were in an auditorium in London in 2024 to pitch their business idea, hoping to secure a full-time job with cosmetics giant L'Oreal."It reminded me of when I used to do competitive sports growing up and the pressure would get heavy," says Liberman, now 24. "But somehow you just get into flow mode."She and her friends had got through to the UK final of Brandstorm, an international competition run by the French company, where young adults outline their product and business ideas.Their proposal for a haircare app saw them crowned UK winners and they went on to that year's global final in Paris where they came third.While only members of the team that finished first automatically got full-time jobs, Liberman had so impressed senior figures at the company that she managed to secure a place on its marketing management traineeship, with a full-time position at the end.Image source, Jon BradleyImage caption, Yumi Liberman, centre, and two friends pitched a business idea to French cosmetics company L'OréalTurning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions, with jobs as the prize, generates publicity and buzz for companies. But for the young people involved, is it exciting - or unfair?In the current global economic environment, youth unemployment is higher than the national average in many countries, as companies are reluctant to take on new staff. In the UK the unemployment rate for young adults is 16.2%,, external compared to the overall level of 4.9%., externalCompetitions like L'Oreal's can offer hope. But the vast majority of the 380,000 people around the world who applied for it this year, up 58% from 240,000 in 2025, didn't win anything.L'Oreal told the BBC that its Brandstorm competition works well because it helps the company attract a wider range of potential new recruits, including young people who wouldn't necessarily have thought of applying for a job at the firm.Yet while Liberman says she enjoyed the formal competition structure, others who have been through similar recruitment competitions are critical.'Intimidating'Melissa Alcruz now works in marketing for a US real estate business based in New York City, but in the past she did the same job for TV channel MTV.While at MTV she competed in an internal competition for a promotion that she says was referred to as a "bake-off". Candidates had to come up with sponsorship and marketing campaigns, and then pitch to a room of seven people."This is intimidating, even for a seasoned professional. I ultimately got the job, but even though I won I disliked the process," says Alcruz.She points out that she already had a demanding full-time role at the company, and was then "expected to complete several substantial projects" for the competition in her spare time.MTV's current parent company, Paramount Skydance Corporation, has been asked for a comment.Former recruitment consultant Katrina Collier, now an author, speaker and recruiter trainer, is concerned that competition-based recruitment processes that potentially require candidates to give up lots of their time for free can create "economic discrimination"."Not everyone can take time, possibly months, to participate in the challenges for the chance to secure one of a limited number of roles," she says. "Does that mean only people from financially strong backgrounds proceed?"Is that leaving talented applicants who don't have the bank of mum or dad, for example, unable to take part?"Image source, Melissa AlcruzImage caption, Melissa Alcruz says that such competitions can require the candidates to have to do too much workJamie Kohn, senior director for talent acquisition at research firm Gartner, reasons that competition-based hiring formats are here to stay because employers find it easier to evaluate candidates than via the traditional interview method.But she agrees that organisations need to be cautious about how much they ask of the jobseekers. "And they should focus on providing feedback… so candidates build their capabilities even if they are not selected."For psychologist Amanda Potter, her concern is that recruiting via competition events tend to favour extroverts, and therefore put quieter personality types at a disadvantage."Does this approach encourage all types of people to apply, or would certain types of people avoid these assessment methods?" she says. "This could result in an organisation [ending up] full of ambitious, competitive people who want to win, possibly to the detriment of others."However, Liberman, who lives with severe dyslexia, argues that going through a typical recruitment process and related assessments would have been more challenging for her.It has also meant that she managed to avoid any time spent unemployed after finishing university. Instead, she has gone straight into her chosen field, something she can't say about all of her peers."I have a lot of friends coming from extremely reputable backgrounds, extremely educated people who have applied to over 1,000 jobs, and have been jobless."

schema.headline: 'I performed on stage to get my first job' - the firms turning recruitment into competitions

title: Courtney Lawes: England legend backs end to overseas player bar
description: England selection should no longer be restricted to players based at domestic clubs, according to cap centurion Courtney Lawes.The 37-year-old is back
body: England selection should no longer be restricted to players based at domestic clubs, according to cap centurion Courtney Lawes.The 37-year-old is back in contention to add to his 105 England appearances, having signed a one-year deal with Sale after two seasons at Brive in the French second tier.A clutch of English talent - notably Toulouse star Jack Willis - remain across the Channel and out of reach for England head coach Steve Borthwick."I can see why they do it because they don't want all their players playing abroad, but I don't think that's necessarily going to be the case anyway," said Lawes."It's important that you have the best players available for selection. If we want the game to develop and more people to watch it, I think it has to develop."I just reckon you make your best players available and by any means necessary."I don't see why you'd limit yourself."In addition to Willis, who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 and could well retain the award after a player-of-the-match performance in the Top 14 final in June, Willis' brother Tom, Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, David Ribbans, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and Junior Kpoku also ply their trade in France.England have better access and control over players who are at Prem clubs. The clubs, in turn, benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) and more chance of retaining their biggest stars, who face international exile with a move overseas.Other nations, such as New Zealand, France and Ireland, have a policy of picking home-based players, but some of England's other rivals, such as South Africa, Australia and Scotland, lean heavily on players based abroad.Borthwick has opted not to include either Lawes or Joe Marchant, his new Sale team-mate who has spent the past three seasons at Stade Francais in Paris, in his first training camp of the season, asking them to prove themselves in the Prem first.The England coach adopted a similar approach when Owen Farrell returned from Racing 92 at the start of last season."I spoke to Steve a little bit," said Lawes, who played 80 minutes in a 50-28 win over Bath in the Prem Rugby Cup on Sunday, to Rugby Union Weekly."It was just what I would expect - he knows I'm coming back and he's going keep an eye on me, but he wants to see me play in the Prem first and I think that's a good idea."I've spent two years away, let's see how I go in the Prem first, I'm not really thinking about England before I can get up and running for Sale so that's there's no point."Lawes, who initially retired from Test rugby after the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final defeat by South Africa, said his return to England was not something he expected when he departed boyhood club Northampton in the wake of lifting the domestic title the following year.

schema.headline: Courtney Lawes: England legend backs end to overseas player bar

title: Champions League 202-27 predictions: Who will win the title?
description: Julien Laurens: If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already specia
body: Julien Laurens: If PSG do the three-peat, it would be an incredible achievement. I don't think they will do it. I think two in a row is already special - three in a row is impossible unless you've got Cristiano Ronaldo in your team, which they don't.I think they will be close. I think they'll reach at least the semi-final, but I think going for three in a row is tough.I don't believe fully in the Jose Mourinho-Real Madrid project, so I would go for Bayern Munich and Arsenal to reach the final. They are probably the teams, other than PSG, who have deserved to be there the most in the past two seasons. To win it, I'll go for Arsenal. They have the best defence in Europe by far and that's what wins you titles. I would go for PSG to reach the last four, Bayern close runners-up and Arsenal to win it.Guillem Balague:With PSG's irregular start to the season we are seeing how difficult it is to maintain the level. Luis Enrique continues to push the team to be in the vanguard of football which is demanding, with dynamic football and relentless pressure. With the league phase considered a place to experiment and prepare for the second half of the season, there will be a time of transition and strange results before the crunch time in January onwards. As the main axis is there, I expect them to get very close to winning it again.But Barcelona are flying. They would like another centre-back and a number nine. It is what Hansi Flick wanted to get to the next level but he feels they are on the way to the top anyway. Arsenal have found a way to win regularly, and with that off their shoulders, players feel a release that will make them play better. Those three should be in the semis unless they meet before. The fourth, again draw permitting, should be Bayern Munich, Real Madrid or Manchester City.Julien Laurens:I have picked five players to watch in this year's Champions League. The first is Jude Bellingham. This is a very big season for him individually and collectively for Real Madrid under Mourinho in the number 10 role that I think suits him well. After a very good World Cup, I think that momentum will carry. I expect him to score a lot of goals and to be very strong and be decisive.Como's number 10 Nico Paz is at the heart of everything they do with the ball. It's their first time in the Champions League. Cesc Fabregas is the manager, so they're a very entertaining team, nice to watch. Paz is a special player - very much in the making - but he will be a top player very soon.Mr Champions League - Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. In the past two seasons, he's been incredible at PSG, especially last year on that left wing where he can cut inside or go on the outside, he's a threat with the right foot and the left foot, he scored some great goals, he's really good technically. I think he's in the running for the Ballon d'Or. He's one of those players that gets you on the edge of your sofa. He's the guy. Lens are back in the Champions League having pushed PSG all the way last year in Ligue 1 - and Ismaelo Ganiou is arguably their best player. A strong centre-back, 21 years old, good on the ball, very quick and physical. I expect him to leave at the end of the season for a big Premier League club.Since leaving Aston Villa to go to Roma, Donyell Malen has been incredible, scoring almost a goal per game as a lone striker for Gian Piero Gasperini's side. Roma being back in the Champions League is great and they're a very entertaining team to watch again. I think we will see Malen back to his best level.Guillem Balague:Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane is in a campaign to win the Ballon d'Or. He deserves to be in contention and I do not expect him to drop his level as Bayern's style suits him greatly.Teenager Lamine Yamal is hungry for more and has set his sights on the Champions League. Hansi Flick wants a team that defends high and passionately so he can shine.Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has got another level and with PSG going far he will again rescue the team and win big games. He will be a Ballon d'Or winner soon.Shakhtar have a long tradition of converting Brazilian stars into European multimillion transfers and 20-year-old Kaua Elias could be the next one on the list.After a difficult season for Martin Odegaard last year with injuries, he has started this one very well. The Norwegian can dominate games, and his team - more confident now - will need him to do that. He seems ready to take that leadership.According to Opta, last year's runners-up Arsenal are the overall favourites to win the Champions League (20.4%) although Bayern Munich, who lost to PSG in the semi-finals, are only marginally behind (20%).PSG's chances of winning a third European title in a row are 7.3%, fourth overall, while 2023 winners Manchester City are third, having been given a 12.7% chance.All five of the Premier League teams are ranked inside the top 10 for overall win probability and all have been given a more than 50% chance of reaching the last-16.When it comes to the league phase, Liverpool have the easiest draw according to Opta's power rankings while Stuttgart have the easiest run overall and Inter Milan the most favourable of the teams from pot one.Arsenal also have a relatively favourable draw. Despite drawing Real Madrid and Bayern Munich from pot one, Mikel Arteta's side also drew the two lowest-ranked sides in the competition - Sabah and Slovan Bratislava.Manchester City face the toughest fixtures of the English clubs with only five teams receiving a tougher draw overall. They have drawn two European giants from pot one in Barcelona and PSG, while 24th-ranked Napoli are a particularly difficult test from pot three.Last season, Arsenal finished top of the league phase after being given one of the easiest fixture lists according to Opta, while Bayern Munich finished second despite being handed the toughest set of opponents of all 36 sides.

schema.headline: Champions League 202-27 predictions: Who will win the title?

title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
description: On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshl
body: On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank."We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April."I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot."When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection."I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades."We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared."They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.  Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that."At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children, external as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham".Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder."In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before."You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said.  "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said."No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting."We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk."Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation".Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents".Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured.Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land.

schema.headline: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
description: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose
body: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos."Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely. It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years. "Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th". OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.  "The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said. Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas.Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility.In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances.The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK.This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history.In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it.The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration.The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him.Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said.Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises

title: New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal links to extremists and Saudi state
description: The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballin
body: The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals.The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy.Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs.The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before.The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania.Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence.This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside.Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody.The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted.He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment.After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden.BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years.Our investigation also found:The plane diagram was sent to the FBI's New York office and was analysed, according to an FBI source. But a US Department of Justice (DOJ) official told the BBC he was never shown a proposal to prosecute Bayoumi based on the evidence, even though "we've convicted people for less"FBI agents in San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the US, repeatedly requested copies of evidence but never received most of itThe San Diego and Los Angeles FBI offices were both blocked from interviewing Bayoumi's Saudi government contactsStaff on the 9/11 Commission objected to the conclusion that Bayoumi was "unlikely" to have been involved with extremists, prompting the report to attribute this to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him"Omar al-Bayoumi arrived in San Diego from Saudi Arabia in 1994. He claimed to be studying English, but court records show that within a few years he had, in effect, abandoned his studies. He was more usually found organising religious events, often with a camcorder pressed to his eye.One video Bayoumi filmed, from 1997 or early 1998, shows men, including Anwar al-Awlaki, paintballing. Filmed near San Diego, the group engages in urban combat scenes and target practice, many wearing military fatigues.At one point, some of the men charge into battle, shouting "Allahu Akbar". A visiting Saudi sheikh is with the group and Bayoumi can also be heard addressing Anwar al-Awlaki with the honorific "Sheikh Anwar".The following morning, in Birmingham, officers began the meticulous process of logging and bagging up evidence in his properties - a cache of many thousands of pages of documents, hundreds of photographs, flight ticket stubs, phone cards, and carrier bags and boxes containing at least 80 videotapes.Within hours of the search starting, several items of documentary evidence - categorised as the highest priority at the direction of the FBI - were taken by police directly to Paddington Green, where the FBI had stationed an agent.This evidence included a phone book containing more than two dozen names of Saudi government officials in the US and Saudi Arabia; flight simulator software; tickets and travel documents; and the yellow lined page of a notebook with the sketch of a plane, which an officer had marked: "contains handwritten notes mathematical calculations re height of planes".Eighteen years later, the FBI would hand the notebook page to the court in the 9/11 families' lawsuit, following a subpoena. The page was made public in 2022."It's the mathematical calculation of the crash," Jodi Westbrook Flowers, a member of the 9/11 families' legal team, told the BBC. "When we figured out what it was, we knew that it was the smoking gun that we'd been looking for."The equation, written in Omar al-Bayoumi's handwriting, indicates the height and distance required for a pilot to guide an aeroplane to a given object on the ground. Underneath it is a small drawing of a plane and a series of numbers.Last year, the federal judge in the families' lawsuit found the notebook page, on the face of it, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks".In 2021, when questioned about it in court, Bayoumi said he had the diagram because he liked finding equations and could not remember when he had written it.By the evening of 22 September 2001, copies of the plane diagram were in London in the hands of both the FBI and UK counter-terror police - and just metres from the custody suite where Omar al-Bayoumi was being questioned. Records show they passed through at least three further FBI agents in the following two days.But here, the mystery begins. The FBI briefed the Met officers to question Bayoumi about the other high-priority exhibits, but the detectives in the custody suite were never given, or briefed about, the plane diagram.Many FBI agents have told us the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was a round-the-clock frenzy. But it is hard to understand how a piece of evidence of this importance, in a case being handled with considerable urgency, was not put into the hands of the interviewing detectives.The FBI declined to respond to our questions. The Metropolitan Police told us it could not comment because of the ongoing legal case.On the day he would need to be charged or released, the Met detectives joined a conference call with several senior officials from the US Department of Justice and FBI.Panorama and Radio 4 have spoken to two participants at the meeting. One recalls the British detectives setting out the evidence they believed met the threshold for the Americans to extradite Bayoumi to face charges in the US.The response from the DOJ officials was that no extradition would be sought because there was insufficient evidence.On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.But, at that point, the FBI had not shipped all of the evidence found in Birmingham back to the US, let alone exhaustively analysed it.One memorandum from the FBI's legal attache in London, sent two weeks later, noted there were a "number of videos, floppy disks and documentation still to be viewed".After Omar al-Bayoumi's release, agents continued analysing the evidence against him.The BBC understands the plane diagram was couriered from London for analysis at the New York Field Office, which was in overall charge of the 9/11 investigation.But we have not been able to trace any records of this analysis or its conclusions. A 2021 Presidential order required the FBI to declassify files relating to its 9/11 investigations, including into Bayoumi.However, of the files released, the FBI has only produced one document referring to the diagram, despite its evidential significance, and this was only created 11 years after the diagram's initial discovery in 2001.The diagram seems to have fallen into a black hole.It was not passed on to San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the USA and where the FBI Field Office was also investigating him.In fact, San Diego - where agents were interviewing his associates, searching his mosque, analysing his telephone records and bank statements - received almost none of the large volume of evidence seized by the Met Police in Birmingham. Rick Lambert, who ran the FBI's investigation there, told the BBC his office made repeated requests to New York to send copies of all the evidence. "Their position was, we're in charge of the case; we'll send it to you when we're finished analysing."Lambert said New York did not comply his office's requests. "I believe there is the potential that had we received that evidence and analysed it, that we would have been able to put the pieces of the puzzle together much more quickly."Documents show that, in spring 2002, the San Diego office was ultimately able to get copies of a handful of videos by obtaining them not from New York, but from the FBI liaison in London.Jeffrey Breinholt, then the deputy director of counter-terrorism at the Department of Justice who oversaw prosecutors working on terrorism charges after 9/11, told the BBC that Bayoumi's name had come up "as one of the hot possibilities for charges".But he said the New York Attorney's Office never sent charges to him or his colleagues for approval. If they had, the plane diagram would have been significant evidence against Bayoumi, he said. "We've convicted people for less."The paintballing video, Breinholt told us, is another "very telling bit of evidence" with the presence of Anwar al-Awlaki being "pretty damn significant"."As a manager who reviewed a lot of proposed terrorism cases over the years, I can tell you that that would have jumped out. I think it would be a material support charge against Bayoumi."There were no charges brought against Bayoumi.Agents who tried to investigate Omar al-Bayoumi encountered other roadblocks.In October 2001 in San Diego, Lambert and colleagues wanted to interview a number of Saudi officials in the US - many connected to the Ministry of Islamic Affairs - who they suspected had co-ordinated the help Bayoumi gave to two of the hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.Because diplomats have a special protected status, the agents needed permission from FBI headquarters and the State Department."The answer came back, 'no, you're not going to do that'," Lambert, who is now a consultant for the 9/11 families in their lawsuit, told us.Agents in Los Angeles experienced a similar outcome the following year, when they applied to interview a Saudi religious diplomat Bayoumi had met immediately after his first encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar in the city."We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns," said Steve Moore, who oversaw the FBI's 9/11 investigation in LA. Moore says his team made repeated requests to interview the official, but permission never came.Like the FBI, the State Department declined to comment.In October 2003, the 9/11 Commission - set up by Congress to provide a "full and complete" account of the attacks - interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi in Riyadh. He had returned to Saudi Arabia in the months after his release by British police.The interview was conducted, in the presence of Saudi secret police, by the Commission's executive director Philip Zelikow, a former advisor to President George W Bush, along with a senior staffer and an agent from FBI headquarters.The Commission's notes from the time record that Bayoumi was given a remarkable degree of reassurance during the interview. He "was told that no-one believes he knowingly helped the hijackers carry out their terrorist mission".Bayoumi indignantly said he was a peace-lover who had become "a victim of the victims". During the interview, the delegation broke away for a multi-course dinner hosted by the Mabahith, the secret police, without Bayoumi.After the interview concluded, the Mabahith told the American delegation they "would like to see him cleared". The Americans responded that no exoneration would be possible before their report was published.When the 9/11 Commission Report was published in July 2004, Bayoumi was, in effect, cleared. It described him as "obliging and gregarious" and stated there was no evidence he had extremist views.But some staff on the Commission were not convinced of Bayoumi's innocence, and thought it likely he knew Hazmi and Mihdhar were al Qaeda operatives.The BBC can reveal that those staff objected to a line in the report concluding that he was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists".In the end, a compromise was agreed, and this conclusion was attributed to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background".The line was written based on the four and a half hours the Commission delegation had spent with Bayoumi, which included the interruption for dinner.The Commission never saw the plane diagram, the paintballing video, written evidence of Bayoumi's alleged extremism, or much of the rest of the evidence the Met Police had seized.Philip Zelikow did not answer the specific questions we asked him. He told the BBC the 9/11 Commission's findings had been subject to two government reviews, in 2015 and 2021, and the Commission had been "open about our suspicions and uncertainties. We were careful about whom to accuse of complicity in mass murder."The Department of Justice told us it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.The head of the FBI's 9/11 investigation, Mary Galligan, has previously stated the Commission had "access to everything".We tried to contact Omar al-Bayoumi through the Saudi government, but he did not respond. He has previously denied knowing Hazmi and Mihdhar were hijackers, that he was a Saudi spy, and that he had any involvement in 9/11.The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia did not respond to our request for comment. It has previously said any allegation that Saudi Arabia or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.

schema.headline: New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal links to extremists and Saudi state

title: Why the ‘Temu Range Rover’ is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover
description: Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has  travelled down a very rough road.The company has seen sales fall in all
body: Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has  travelled down a very rough road.The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year. At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands. Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles. JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles. This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins. All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled – a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese  firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad. They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe – with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover'  the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year. Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.The US is also a major market for JLR. In the year to the end of March 2025 it sold more than 120,000 cars there. The following year, that figure had fallen to just under 100,000. Part of that could be attributed to the impact of the cyber attack, which heavily disrupted production in late 2025. It affected JLR worldwide and cost the company £1.9bn. But sales and profits were also hit by the introduction of import tariffs by the US, and subsequent uncertainty over the levels of those tariffs. As automotive analyst Matthias Schmidt puts it, the company is "seeing a head-on hit each time a Land Rover rolls off a ship onto US soil".JLR is now planning a partnership with Stellantis to build new Defender-badged vehicles in the US. These cars, which would be developed specifically for the US market, would not attract tariffs.Then, there are energy costs, which affect JLR and its rivals. Carmakers and their suppliers are industrial businesses that use copious amounts of energy, and prices in the UK are among the highest in Europe. According to Prof David Bailey of Birmingham Business School, "electricity is a fundamental input into modern industrial production"."If producing a car in Britain is structurally more expensive because the energy required to manufacture it is substantially more expensive, Britain is effectively imposing a competitiveness tax on its own industry."All of these challenges have come at a time when JLR has been ploughing money into the development of a new generation of electric vehicles. The first fruits of the £15bn programme were seen last week, with the official unveiling of the first electric Range Rover. That was relatively uncontroversial – but so far the relaunch of Jaguar as an all-electric brand has been anything but. In late 2024 the company drove straight into the heart of the culture wars with a polarising advertising campaign that some saw as excessively "woke". The first actual car is due to make its public bow on 6 October – and it will be a pivotal moment for the company.It is easy to see why JLR's chief executive PJ Balaji feels action is necessary to trim costs and make the company leaner. That is bad news for employees, with thousands of jobs to go and compulsory redundancies not being ruled out.But the carmaker's network of suppliers are also being squeezed. "JLR has been pushing hard for cost savings", one leading supplier told the BBC. "But those suppliers are also facing high energy costs and high employment costs…there's huge anxiety right now."

schema.headline: Why the ‘Temu Range Rover’ is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover

title: UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements
description: The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.For
body: The UK government is to set out new restrictions on buying goods made in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the BBC understands.Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is expected to outline the measures in the Commons on Tuesday, which could include restrictions on trade in agricultural products from settlements.Last week, Miliband said he would unveil a "comprehensive reset" of the British government's policy on Israel.The Israeli government has previously warned it would retaliate if any new measures were introduced.Settlements are illegal under international law, and recent months have seen a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers.One minister told the BBC: "The statement will be a complete reset of the nature of our Israel-Palestine relationship. It will all feel very different."It is not just about sanctions. We hope that this will finally achieve what those of us who have been working towards for two years over the Middle East have been working on."BBC News has not seen the full details of the measures.But Labour MPs who have been briefed on the plans believe the sanctions will target trade with illegal settlements. They believe that means the sanctions would cover both goods and services.Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed to Labour MPs at their weekly parliamentary meeting on Monday night that Miliband would be making the statement, according to a number of MPs present.The prime minister is also said to have told the meeting that he had briefed international leaders about plans in phone calls on Monday afternoon.Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump over the phone on Monday, during which the prime minister stressed the importance of a two-state solution in the Middle East.An official account of the call released by No 10 did not specify that Burnham had briefed Trump on the sanctions, while the US - which is likely to strongly oppose the proposals - has not commented.Speaking in July, Stephen Doughty - who was then Europe minister but has since been appointed Middle East minister - told the business select committee that existing powers to impose restrictions on settlements did not go far enough.He said: "At the moment, we can sanction where there is evidence of it being linked to settler violence, but not, for example, in relation to a contractor working on the settlements. We need to expand our sanctions powers."While ministers are said to recognise that banning a relatively small quantity of mostly agricultural products is a largely symbolic gesture, the government is expected to frame this announcement as a major reset in Britain's wider policy on Israel.The expected announcement by the UK government comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.Speaking in his first address to Parliament as foreign secretary last week, Miliband said those plans were "illegal under international law", and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's announcement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.Tuesday's expected intervention will come almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.The government believes the prospect of a two-state solution is being jeopardised by the rapid expansion of settlements. The proposal for an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital, to exist alongside Israel has received international backing over several decades. Israel rejects a two-state solution. The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

schema.headline: UK government expected to announce restrictions on trade with West Bank settlements

title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September."While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.'Significant distress'The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new ownersTwo data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community"."Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

schema.headline: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status

title: Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
description: Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.It follows a sear
body: Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country. In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union. Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.

schema.headline: Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
